question: to the Commission Anna Maria Cisint (PfE) Subject:

A recent report by the organisation Foodwatch has shed light on a serious problem affecting the food safety of European citizens. Residues of pesticides banned in the EU have been found in 14 foodstuffs sold in France, Germany and Austria, including a well-known brand of Thai rice. This is yet more evidence of need for an overhaul of our monitoring system and the fallibility of our safeguard mechanisms, undermining the principle of reciprocity. Instead, the Commission would be well advised to change its approach and instead ensure the automatic alignment of maximum residue levels (MRLs) for imported products, granting limited derogations in exceptional cases, subject to compliance with food-safety criteria. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.
How it intends to prioritise the need to protect European rice, by means of the monitoring system and the measures set out in the ‘food and feed safety’ omnibus package currently under negotiation.

Whether it considers it useful, pending the final revision of the rules, to implement a system for verifying alternative substances which, in the interests of ensuring genuine sustainability, is compatible with safeguarding the potential yield and strategic role of agricultural districts, such as those that produce rice.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.9.2026) Pesticide residues in food placed on the EU market, whether produced in the EU or imported, are subject to strict rules, including the setting of maximum residue levels (MRLs)1, and are systematically monitored by the Member States’ competent authorities. The results are summarised in annual reports by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). EFSA’s latest report2 shows a 98.2% compliance rate with MRLs based on 86,449 samples analysed across a wide range of products in the Member States. When non-compliances are detected, Member State authorities take measures that are proportionate to the risk for consumers. Noncompliant goods are either stopped at the border and not allowed on the EU market or withdrawn from it. In addition to the current EU monitoring and enforcement framework, the Commission launched in January 2026 a Task Force on Import Controls3 to improve the harmonised implementation of import controls across the EU, including for pesticide residues, and to ensure that food placed on the EU market is safe. The Food and Feed Simplification Package4 aims to stimulate innovation and accelerate market access for new biocontrol substances and plant protection products (PPPs) containing them while ensuring that farmers have access to essential PPPs for which alternatives are not available, especially when a serious danger to plant production is identified5. The Commission has also proposed that Member States can grant longer grace periods for distribution and use of existing stocks of PPPs when their authorisations must be withdrawn. During the negotiation of the proposed Package, the Commission and the Member States remain bound by the current legislative framework.
1 Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 February 2005 on

maximum residue levels of pesticides in or on food and feed of plant and animal origin and amending Council Directive 91/414/EEC, OJ L 70, 16.3.2005. 2 https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2026.10054. 3 Import controls of food and feed Q&As - Food Safety: https://food.ec.europa.eu/horizontal-topics/officialcontrols-and-enforcement/import-controls-food-and-feed-qas_en. 4 https://food.ec.europa.eu/horizontal-topics/simplification-legislation_en. 5 For this purpose, the Commission has proposed amendment to Article 4(7) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009.
